walkthroughs.body_html:
Area of Study 1: Instrumental Music of Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven — a core area of A-Level Music.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Area of Study 1: Instrumental Music of Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Area of Study 1: Instrumental Music of Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What distinguishes Classical (1750-1820) from Baroque style?
options: It is the very first section.
Use of orchestra (Baroque had none).
Classical means any old serious music.
Clearer melodic phrases, homophonic texture, balanced structures like sonata form.

mcqs.q: How does D Dorian differ from D minor?
options: Dorian has no sharps or flats at all.
Classical means any old serious music.
They are the same scale.
Dorian has a raised 6th (B natural) compared to natural minor.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Serialism”?
options: Compositional method using a fixed ordering of all twelve chromatic pitches, developed by Schoenberg around 1923.
Late twentieth-century approach analysing the acoustic spectrum of sound, developed by Grisey and Murail in 1970s France.
Style emerging in the 1960s using repetition and gradual process, exemplified by Steve Reich and Philip Glass.
Music without a tonal centre, pioneered by Schoenberg around 1908 in works such as the Three Piano Pieces Op. 11.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Minimalism”?
options: Music incorporating chance elements, associated with John Cage's '4'33"' (1952) and Lutoslawski.
Style emerging in the 1960s using repetition and gradual process, exemplified by Steve Reich and Philip Glass.
Compositional method using a fixed ordering of all twelve chromatic pitches, developed by Schoenberg around 1923.
Style using recorded environmental and instrumental sounds as raw material, founded by Pierre Schaeffer in 1948.
